questions.title: How can an individual plaintiff maintain Article III standing to seek statutory penalties that are payable directly to the state Commissioner rather than the plaintiff?
questions.question_body: The court discusses *Friends of the Earth* and notes that civil penalties paid to the government 'may afford redress' by deterring future violations. However, the opinion explicitly states that under the MFLSA, these penalties go to the Commissioner, not Cohen. Since Cohen has already been fully compensated for his own wages and liquidated damages, what specific 'personal stake' or 'concrete injury' allows him to satisfy the standing requirement for a claim where he receives zero dollars? Does the threat of a penalty against the employer count as a cognizable injury to Cohen personally?

questions.title: Does the doctrine of voluntary cessation allow a federal court to proceed with summary judgment on an MFLSA claim when the employer has stopped paying but hasn't formally withdrawn its policy?
questions.question_body: The court vacates and remands because there is a factual dispute over whether Consilio's new overtime policy is still in place. If Consilio simply stops enforcing the policy after being sued (voluntary cessation), doesn't *City of Mesquite v. Aladdin's Castle* generally prevent mootness unless it is 'absolutely clear' that the conduct cannot recur? Why didn't the Eighth Circuit just rule on whether the policy was still active based on existing evidence, rather than sending it back solely to determine jurisdiction/mootness?

questions.title: What is the precise distinction between an employee's right to sue for wages versus their right to sue for penalties under Minn. Stat. § 181.101 of the MPWA?
questions.question_body: The court affirms summary judgment on Cohen's MPWA claim because § 181.101 only allows private suits for wages, reserving penalties for the Commissioner after they serve a demand letter. The opinion cites *Allan v. R.D. Offutt Co.* regarding plain language interpretation. Can someone clarify why § 181.101(a) creates this bifurcation where an employee can prosecute a claim for wages but cannot initiate a suit for penalties themselves? Is this purely statutory text limitation or does it involve separation of powers concerns regarding who enforces labor laws?

questions.title: Is an appellate court permitted to affirm a lower court's dismissal of a claim without addressing it if the appellant fails to cite specific statutory authority supporting their position?
questions.question_body: Regarding Cohen's MWTA claim, he complained that Consilio failed to provide notice of policy changes and sought penalties. The appellate court affirmed dismissal simply stating Cohen 'points to no statutory authority allowing for civil penalties under this statute.' Given that Cohen listed multiple statutes in his initial complaint, isn't there a risk that he waived his argument by failing to include specific legal citations or arguments in his brief? How strictly does Rule 28 require appellants to link their specific relief requests (penalties) to specific subsections of statutes?

questions.title: Can an appellant raise a new theory of injunctive relief in their opening brief after withdrawing earlier requests during summary judgment briefing?
questions.question_body: Cohen originally sought specific injunctive relief in his complaint but withdrew those requests and asked for something different ('rescind its illegal overtime policy') only during his summary judgment opposition brief. The district court ignored this change, and now the appellate court says this issue is 'not properly before us.' Why is changing theories at this late stage fatal? Shouldn't Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(a) allow amendments, or does raising it for the first time in an appeal brief constitute waiver regardless of whether an amendment was filed?

questions.title: If a defendant pays all owed damages before summary judgment, does that automatically moot all claims except those involving public enforcement mechanisms like fines or penalties?
questions.question_body: In this case, Consilio paid Cohen every penny he was owed plus liquidated damages under MFLSA before filing their motion for summary judgment. The court treats this payment as resolving all personal monetary claims but leaving open potential claims for statutory penalties payable to the state. Does full satisfaction of damages always moot private rights of action unless there is some unique feature (like treble damages retained by plaintiff or public interest factors)? Or does full payment never moot a case if there are ancillary claims like attorney's fees or declaratory judgments pending?
